# Psalm 44 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview and Setting

**Title and Authorship:** The title reads "For the choirmaster. A Maskil of the sons of Korah." Spurgeon notes the title is similar to Psalm 42 and though he is reluctant to ascribe it to anyone but David, "hardly know any period of his life which it would fairly describe," so he concludes some "Israelitish patriot fallen on evil times" wrote it (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps044.php). Gill notes the Targum ascribes it to David, but says David may have "under a prophetic influence" spoken of future times (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/44.htm). Ellicott places it in the post-exilic period, with the majority of critics preferring "the time of Antiochus Epiphanes" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/44.htm).

**Structure:** The psalm divides into four parts: (1) remembrance of God's past victories (vv. 1–3); (2) confident prayer for present help (vv. 4–8); (3) the complaint of present defeat (vv. 9–16); (4) protest of innocence and plea for deliverance (vv. 17–26).

---

## Verses 1–3: Remembering God's Past Victories

**v. 1 – "We have heard with our ears, O God; our fathers have told us the work You did in their days…"**

- **Gill:** The church in distress recalls past favours to encourage faith. The expression "heard with our ears" shows "the clearness, evidence, and certainty of what was heard," transmitted not just orally but through the written record of Moses and the prophets read publicly and privately (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/44.htm).
- **Spurgeon:** God's mighty acts were "subjects of common conversation," preserved by oral tradition with "great diligence and accuracy." He adds: "When fathers are tongue tied religiously with their offspring, need they wonder if their children's hearts remain sin tied?" (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps044.php).
- **Bible.org (Bob Utley):** The Jewish annual feasts were the occasions for instructing new generations about God's saving acts (cf. Exod 12; Deut 6:20-25). "It is the spiritual responsibility of every generation of believers to instruct the new generation about God, His character, and redemptive acts" (https://new.bible.org/seriespage/psalm-44).

**v. 2 – "With Your hand You drove out the nations and planted our fathers there; You crushed the peoples and cast them out."**

- **Ellicott:** The Hebrew word rendered "cast them out" actually means a tree "spreading its branches out" (cf. Ps 80:11). The correct sense is: "Thou, with thine hand, didst dispossess the heathen, and planted them (Israel) in. Thou didst afflict the peoples, but didst make them to spread" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/44.htm).
- **Gill:** "The Canaanites" were driven out and Israel was "planted" like a vine; the metaphor of planting Israel appears in Exod 15:17 and Jer 2:21 (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/44.htm).
- **Utley (bible.org):** 44:2 refers to the native tribes of Canaan. The OT viewed YHWH as the establisher of all people groups; the Canaanites were expelled "because of their sins" (https://new.bible.org/seriespage/psalm-44).

**v. 3 – "It was not by their sword that they took the land…It was by Your right hand, Your arm, and the light of Your face, because You favored them."**

- **Guzik (Enduring Word):** The fathers' stories created an expectation that God acts the same way in every era—"like our reflection on the Protestant Reformation or Great Awakenings" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-44/).
- **Utley:** The conquest "fulfilled the promise of Gen. 15:12-21." The threefold parallel—"Your right hand," "Your arm," "the light of Your presence"—with the third referring to the Shekinah Cloud of Glory during the wilderness period. The verb "favored" denotes God's covenant purpose of bringing all peoples to Himself through Abraham's seed (https://new.bible.org/seriespage/psalm-44).
- **Ellicott:** Notes the contrast to v. 24—"in times of distress God's face seemed hidden or averted" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/44.htm).

---

## Verses 4–8: Confident Prayer for Present Victory

**v. 4 – "You are my King, O God, who ordains victories for Jacob."**

- **Ellicott:** The Hebrew reads literally "Thou, He, my king"—"an idiomatic way of making a strong assertion, Thou, even thou, art my king, O God." What God did in the past may be expected again (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/44.htm).
- **Utley:** YHWH as King probably derives from 1 Sam 8:7; the Israelite king "was only an earthly representative of YHWH's rule and reign." The word "victories" is literally "salvation" (yeshuah), which "in the OT denotes deliverance from physical problems and enemies" (https://new.bible.org/seriespage/psalm-44).
- **Gill:** The church claims her interest in God as King, who can "by a word of his…command deliverances for Jacob"—the spiritual Jacob, "all Israelites indeed, in whom there is no guile" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/44.htm).

**v. 5 – "Through You we repel our foes; through Your name we trample our enemies."**

- **Ellicott:** The image is of "a buffalo or other horned animal driving back and goring its enemies." Deuteronomy 33:17 applies this as a special description of the tribe of Joseph. The figure continues in the next clause: "the infuriated animal tramples its victim under foot" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/44.htm).
- **Gill:** The Chaldee paraphrase renders it "through the Word"—"the essential Word of God, the Lord Jesus Christ." The metaphor comes from "creatures pushing with their horns" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/44.htm).

**v. 6 – "For I do not trust in my bow, nor does my sword save me."**

- **Gill:** "In any carnal weapon, in any creature help and assistance, or in an arm of flesh, but in the word of the Lord." He adds: "the church's weapons are not carnal, but spiritual; not the sword of the civil magistrate, but the sword of the Spirit" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/44.htm).
- **Guzik:** The shift to "I" (singular) in a national psalm may indicate the psalmist speaking as representative of the nation, or the personal appropriation of national faith (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-44/).

**v. 7 – "For You save us from our enemies; You put those who hate us to shame."**

- **Gill:** God saves from spiritual enemies, "not we ourselves; and therefore will not trust in ourselves…but in the Lord, and give him the glory of salvation" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/44.htm).

**v. 8 – "In God we have boasted all day long, and Your name we will praise forever. Selah."**

- **Utley:** Notes the parallelism: "boasted — give thanks," and "all day long — forever." Selah probably marks a musical pause or interlude (https://new.bible.org/seriespage/psalm-44).
- **Gill:** The Targum renders it "in the word of the Lord"—"in Christ, who is God over all, and who of God is made to his church and people wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/44.htm).

---

## Verses 9–16: The Complaint of Present Defeat

**v. 9 – "But You have rejected and humbled us; You no longer go forth with our armies."**

- **Guzik:** The psalmist now states his "great present need." They felt God no longer fought for Israel, so they were "without hope in battle. The key to prevailing over their enemies was to first prevail with God" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-44/).
- **Utley:** This strophe is a "stark reversal" of vv. 1–3 and 4–8. Instead of YHWH fighting for Israel, "He is fighting against them." The reason is "covenant disobedience and its consequences (cf. Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 27–30)" (https://new.bible.org/seriespage/psalm-44).
- **The Pulpit Commentary (Homiletics):** Notes the historical pathos: after Culloden, a soldier of Prince Charles's army was found dead with his Gaelic psalm-book open and a bloody finger-mark at this verse—"But thou hast cast off, and put us to shame, and goest not forth with our armies" (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/psalms/44.htm).

**v. 10 – "You have made us retreat from the foe, and those who hate us have plundered us."**

- **Ellicott:** "For themselves" means "at their own will"—an expression "denoting the completeness of the overthrow of the Jews; they lie absolutely at their enemies' pleasure" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/44.htm).

**v. 11 – "You have given us up as sheep to be devoured; You have scattered us among the nations."**

- **Guzik:** The psalmist understood that for Israel as a covenant nation, "victory or defeat was in the hand of the LORD." He highlights the "repetition of the word You"—blame is placed squarely on God, not on enemies (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-44/).
- **Ellicott:** The sheep image "recalls Isaiah 53:6-7, but does not necessarily connect the Psalm with the exile period, since it was a figure likely to suggest itself in every time of helpless peril" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/44.htm).

**v. 12 – "You sell Your people for nothing; no profit do You gain from their sale."**

- **Pulpit Commentary (Homiletics):** This is one of the psalm's great arguments: "It would bring no profit or honour to God. To leave them to their enemies. How could God act thus, so as to seem to dishonour himself and to bring no profit to his people?" (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/psalms/44.htm).
- **Ellicott:** "For nought" is literally "for not riches" (cf. Jer 15:13). He suggests the second clause means "thou didst not set a high price on them" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/44.htm).

**v. 13–14 – "You have made us a reproach…a byword among the nations, a laughingstock among the peoples."**

- **Ellicott:** These verses become "very suggestive" if referred to periods under the Seleucids when Jews were attacked on the Sabbath and would make no resistance. He quotes Robert Browning's *Holy Cross Day*: "By the torture, prolonged from age to age, By the infamy, Israel's heritage…" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/44.htm).

**vv. 15–16 – "All day long my disgrace is before me…at the voice of the scorner and reviler, because of the enemy, bent on revenge."**

- **Gill:** "Not by reason of sin…but on account of what follows"—the reproach and blasphemy of the enemy. He identifies the enemy and avenger with "antichrist, who is the enemy of Christ and of his people" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/44.htm).

---

## Verses 17–19: Protest of Innocence

**v. 17 – "All this has come upon us, though we have not forgotten You or betrayed Your covenant."**

- **Guzik:** This is "an honest, anti-penitential psalm." The psalmist is not self-righteous but "honestly (and not self-righteously) makes the case that their present distress was not due to unaddressed sin or rebellion." He cites G. Campbell Morgan: "The arresting fact is, that here is a song revealing an experience of defeat and humiliation…for which no cause is to be found in the conduct of the sufferers" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-44/).
- **Utley:** Israel claims innocence on four counts: not forgotten God, not dealt falsely with His covenant, heart not turned back, steps not deviated. But Utley cautions: "This may be true for some Israelites but not for the majority of them, for the majority of their history (cf. Deuteronomy 32; Psalm 78; Nehemiah 9)" (https://new.bible.org/seriespage/psalm-44).
- **Pulpit Commentary (Homiletics):** The argument is: "It could not be a punishment for unfaithfulness. They had not forgotten God; their heart was not turned back…They could not explain" (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/psalms/44.htm).

**v. 18 – "Our hearts have not turned back; our steps have not strayed from Your path."**

- **Gill:** Their trials had "no such influence upon them as to cause them to apostatize from God, neither in heart, nor in action" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/44.htm).

**v. 19 – "But You have crushed us in the lair of jackals; You have covered us with deepest darkness."**

- **Ellicott:** "The place of dragons" (KJV) / "jackals" means "a wild desert place" (cf. Jer 9:11; 10:22). The jackal "utters a mournful howl" (cf. Mic 1:8; Job 30:29). The LXX and Vulgate render it "in the place of affliction" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/44.htm).
- **Utley:** "YHWH has abandoned His covenant people to the demonic forces of pagan religions and the realm of death!" The "shadow of death" recalls Ps 23:4. Utley says this verse is "theologically similar to Job where he was willing to make God look bad to enhance his own case" (https://new.bible.org/seriespage/psalm-44).
- **Guzik:** In "firm but polite protest," the psalmist insists that "Israel's faithfulness to God had been answered by disaster sent by God" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-44/).

---

## Verses 20–22: The Mystery of Suffering for God's Sake

**vv. 20–21 – "If we had forgotten the name of our God or spread out our hands to a foreign god, would not God have discovered, since He knows the secrets of the heart?"**

- **Spurgeon:** "An appeal is now made to the omniscience of God; he is himself called in to bear witness that Israel had not set up another God." Stretching out hands was "the symbol of adoration or of entreaty in prayer." The reasoning is that "the Lord himself knew the people to be sincerely his followers, and therefore was not visiting them for sin; hence…affliction evidently came from quite another cause" (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps044.php).
- **Gill:** This is "an appeal to God for the truth of all that the church had said concerning her steadfastness and integrity under the most trying exercises" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/44.htm).
- **Utley:** A "specific denial of idolatry." If they were idolatrous, YHWH would surely have known (cf. Ps 7:9; 17:3; 139:23; Jer 17:10) (https://new.bible.org/seriespage/psalm-44).

**v. 22 – "Yet for Your sake we face death all day long; we are considered as sheep to be slaughtered."**

- **Guzik:** *"For Your sake* are the important words. It means that they suffered in faithfulness to God, and because of their faithfulness to God." Quoting Derek Kidner: suffering may be "the price of loyalty in a world which is at war with God" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-44/).
- **Pulpit Commentary:** "Not only are the Israelites not suffering on account of any previous desertion of God…but they are suffering for their fidelity to God. The heathen hate them…as worshippers of one exclusive God, Jehovah." They are "martyrs, like the Christians of the early Church" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/44-22.htm).
- **Spurgeon:** "Persecution never ceased to hound them to the death, they had no respite and found no door of escape; and all in God's behalf, because they would not forsake their covenant God and King." He adds: "From Piedmont and Smithfield, from St. Bartholomew's massacre and the dragoonades of Claverhouse, this appeal goes up to heaven" (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps044.php).
- **Utley:** Paul's use of this verse in Rom 8:36 "seems to indicate that God's people face problems in a fallen world but He is with them and for them. Nothing can separate us from God's love in Christ (cf. Rom. 8:38-39)." Utley is cautious about making "for Your sake" the key theological thrust of the psalm: "I am just not sure there is enough textual evidence from this Psalm to make this claim!" (https://new.bible.org/seriespage/psalm-44).
- **Gill:** These words "had their accomplishment in the ten persecutions under the Heathen emperors, and under the Papal tyranny" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/44.htm).

---

## Verses 23–26: Urgent Plea for God to Act

**v. 23 – "Wake up, O Lord! Why are You sleeping? Arise! Do not reject us forever."**

- **Utley:** "This is an idiomatic anthropomorphic phrase (cf. Ps. 78:65). YHWH (here called Adonai) does not sleep (cf. Ps. 121:4), but at times because of Israel's sin, He seems to remove Himself from fellowship with them" (https://new.bible.org/seriespage/psalm-44).
- **Spurgeon:** "God sleepeth not, but the psalmist puts it so, as if on no other theory he could explain the divine inaction. He would fain see the great Judge ending oppression and giving peace to the holy" (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps044.php).
- **Ellicott:** Cross-references Ps 7:6 and similar calls for God to "awake" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/44.htm).

**v. 24 – "Why do You hide Your face and forget our affliction and oppression?"**

- **Spurgeon:** "Not petulantly, but piteously and inquiringly, we may question the Lord when his dealings are mysterious. We are permitted to order our case with arguments, and plead the right before the face of the august Majesty." He adds: "This question is far more easily asked than answered" (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps044.php).
- **Utley:** "'Forever' is another idiom referring to fellowship (cf. Ps. 103:9). It seemed forever to them! But it was simply a period of disfellowship so as to engender repentance and restore long term fellowship" (https://new.bible.org/seriespage/psalm-44).

**v. 25 – "For our soul has sunk to the dust; our bodies cling to the earth."**

- **Spurgeon:** "Our heart is low as low can be, as low as the dust beneath the soles of men's feet. When the heart sinks, the man is down indeed." On "our belly cleaveth unto the earth": "The man is prone upon the earth, and he is not only down, but fastened down on the earth and glued to it." Yet he adds: "God's saints may be thus abject…but their day cometh, and their tide will turn, and they shall have a brave summer after their bitter winter" (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps044.php).
- **Utley:** This is "imagery for people praying, either on their knees or prostrate on the ground"—an unusual posture of prayer (normally standing with hands lifted), denoting intensity (https://new.bible.org/seriespage/psalm-44).

**v. 26 – "Rise up; be our help! Redeem us on account of Your loving devotion."**

- **Guzik:** "The psalmist has stated Israel's problem as clearly and strongly as possible. We might expect him to be angry with God or to lose hope. Instead the psalm leaves him with trusting God even in his pain and disappointment. He made his final appeal not on the basis of what Israel deserved, but for the sake of God's mercy (lovingkindness)" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-44/).
- **Spurgeon:** "A short, but sweet and comprehensive prayer, much to the point, clear, simple, urgent, as all prayers should be." On "for thy mercies' sake": "The favour is redemption, the plea is mercy; and this, too, in the case of faithful sufferers who had not forgotten their God. Mercy is always a safe plea, and never will any man find a better" (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps044.php).
- **Utley:** YHWH acts "not because of Israel's goodness (cf. Deut. 9:4-6; Ezek. 36:22-38)" but for His covenant loyalty (hesed) to His word (https://new.bible.org/seriespage/psalm-44).

---

## Distinctive Protestant Traditions

### Reformed / Presbyterian (Ligonier)
The Ligonier devotional sees the psalm in three parts: (1) record of God's past mercy; (2) complaint that God has not been favorable as before; (3) the faithful remnant's claim that suffering is *due to* their steadfast devotion, not sin. It stresses that "believers who hold fast to true religion are oftentimes subject to persecutions for Christ's sake" and that Paul in Romans 8:36 "affirmed that this is the state of the church in all ages." The application is that "the cup God has given us to drink contains suffering, and we must be willing to drink it or prove ourselves to be goats among the flock of God" (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/sheep-for-the-slaughter).

### Baptist (Spurgeon)
Spurgeon interprets the psalm Christologically—the church under persecution. He identifies the speakers as the "saved by grace, the sons of Korah" and says "by Christians it can best be understood if put into the mouth of the church when persecution is peculiarly severe." He references the Protestant massacres explicitly—Piedmont, Smithfield, St. Bartholomew's—and treats v. 22 as "the martyr's cry." For Spurgeon, the psalm is not about Israel's historical crisis but a pattern for the suffering church of all ages (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps044.php).

### Baptist (Gill)
Gill takes the psalm as applying primarily to "the times of the New Testament" and reads it through an anti-Catholic polemical lens: the "Heathen" among whom Israel is scattered become "the Papacy," and the "enemy and avenger" becomes "antichrist." Yet he also reads the psalm Christologically: "through the Word" (the essential Word, Christ) we push down enemies. His overall approach is to see the psalm as describing the suffering of the true church under both pagan Rome and papal Rome (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/44.htm).

### Evangelical / Baptist (Bob Utley, bible.org)
Utley is more cautious. He acknowledges the psalm is national and post-exilic, and that the problem is fundamentally "covenant disobedience and its consequences." He is reluctant to fully endorse the "righteous sufferer" interpretation of v. 22, noting "I am just not sure there is enough textual evidence from this Psalm to make this claim." He allows that it may describe a faithful remnant but insists "this may be true for some Israelites but not for the majority." This represents a more historically-literal and less typological Baptist reading (https://new.bible.org/seriespage/psalm-44).

### Pentecostal / Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik)
Guzik emphasizes the emotional and experiential dimension: the psalm as "honest, anti-penitential" protest, where the sufferer boldly states the pain without self-blame. He stresses the revolutionary concept that "suffering may not be a punishment, but a battle scar." His application is pastoral: "When we face unexplained suffering despite our faithfulness to God, we can follow the psalmist's example: state the pain honestly, protest before God without shame, and appeal to His mercy alone rather than claim we deserve deliverance" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-44/).

---

## Other Views

### Modern Scholarship (NET Bible notes — via bible.org's references)
Utley's commentary interacts with the NET Bible and modern textual criticism. The UBS Text Project gives "jackal" (v. 19) a "B" rating (some doubt), with the alternate reading "sea monster" (tannîn). The Canaanite background associates desert creatures with "the demonic of a nation" (cf. Isa 13:21-22; 34:11-15) (https://new.bible.org/seriespage/psalm-44).

### Anglican / Older Critical (Ellicott)
Ellicott places the psalm in the Maccabean period (time of Antiochus Epiphanes), noting that it "might well have been inspired by one of those reverses, which so often came upon the struggling community of Israel, in consequence of their scrupulous concern for the Sabbath day, which did not even allow them to defend themselves." This is a distinct historical-critical dating that differs from conservative Protestant views which tend to date it earlier (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/44.htm).

### Early Church / Patristic (via Gill and Spurgeon references)
Gill cites Theodoret (5th-century bishop) who also saw the psalm as prophetically speaking "of the times of the Maccabees and of Antiochus, when the church and people of God suffered much for the true religion, and abode steadfast in it" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/44.htm).

### Romans 8:36 Quotation (Cross-tradition agreement)
All traditions agree on the significance of Paul's quotation of v. 22 in Romans 8:36. The Reformed (Ligonier), Baptist (Spurgeon, Gill), Pentecostal (Guzik), and Evangelical (Utley) sources all note that Paul uses the verse to show that even in catastrophic defeat, nothing can separate believers from the love of Christ. This is one of the most universally agreed-upon interpretive points across all Protestant traditions for this psalm.
